B.2 Baseline Implementations Offline Verification. TRM scores the trajectory from 1 to 5 in a single call from the instruction, every thought and action, and the last three frames; CUAJudge checks up to six task-derived key points against the first and last of up to six frames in a single call; OS-Themis verifies up to four ordered milestones over up to eight frames and reviews them in a second call. The three offline judges run under one harness at temperature 0, with images downsampled to a long side of 1280 pixels, the first and last frames pinned, no self-consistency voting, and a parse failure mapped to fail . TRM thresholds its 1–5 score at 4 and is the only judge that sees the agent’s thoughts. CUAJudge collapses the original four-stage pipeline into one call, dropping the dedicated frame-selection and init-versus-final modules. OS-Themis collapses the multi-agent critic to two calls with the budget cut to four milestones and eight frames against the original six and twelve; Table C.6 shows that restoring the original budget changes little. Online Environments. The online VLM judge answers in one word from the instruction and the final screenshot and never abstains; the auto-generated verifier writes one evaluator script per task with full device access and runs it once. The auto-generated verifier receives the instruction with its concrete parameters, the same generic device context our synthesis receives, unrestricted host-side adb and Python, and the agent’s submitted answer on answer-scored tasks. It does not receive the trajectory, the results of context inspection, or the pre-state anchor, and it runs last on each end state. Majority Voting. Majority voting combines the same three verifier draws by vote with abstentions folded to fail . B.3 Verifier Configuration Offline Verification. The default runs K = 3 K=3 paths and stops after two when they agree on the status of every hard requirement, which happens on about two fifths of the trajectories. A path spends up to four tool calls gathering support and then at least four, or two per hard requirement, hunting refutations. Each call returns one observation, frames are downscaled to at most 1288 pixels on the long side, and only the last eight images stay in context. The rubric comes from three candidate decompositions consolidated in a fourth call. The sealed initial judgment reads the last five frames together with the thought and action log and is reused only as the fallback. Online Environments. Rubric synthesis draws two candidate rubrics at temperature 0.7 and consolidates them in a third call at temperature 0; checker synthesis makes two parallel calls at temperature 0.7 and asks for two checkers per hard requirement on different surfaces where the state allows it; context inspection uses one call over at most three packages and six databases, followed by one schema probe; a semantic predicate costs one judge call at temperature 0 over at most three images. No call carries a token cap, and each has a 180-second timeout with up to six retries. B.4 Evaluation Metrics The binary evaluation treats success as the positive class. Abstentions are counted as fail for agreement, precision, recall, F1, and the false positive rate. For verifiers that abstain, we also report the decision rate and the accuracy on decided episodes. Appendix E Limitations and Broader Impacts VeriCUA trades cost for evidence. A verification pass issues tens of tool calls and model calls per trajectory, an order of magnitude more than a single-call judge, so it suits filtering and reward assignment better than interactive use. On recorded trajectories it abstains wherever the recording holds no evidence for a requirement. Those abstentions are a coverage limit, and online access lifts it only for environments that can be instrumented. A stochastic verifier also needs its draw-to-draw spread reported beside every comparison, as we do. Reliable trajectory verification lowers the cost of training computer-using agents and of auditing benchmark labels. The same machinery could be misused to certify agents that act on real systems, which is one reason VeriCUA never writes to the environment it verifies.
